Artificial Intelligence.summary: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 43 pages, 11 figures, 13 tables. PACE Reviewer Checklist, evaluation utilities (pace CLI), and reproduction data at https://github.com/mahmoudsajjadi/pace

Artificial Intelligence.title: LEGAL-UQA: Testing Constitutional Question-Answering Systems for Urdu Speakers with a Parallel English-Urdu Benchmark
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Legal information assistants could help Urdu speakers understand their constitutional rights, but building reliable systems requires test data and evaluation methods suited to the language. We present LEGAL-UQA, a parallel English-Urdu benchmark of 619 question-answer pairs linked to passages from Pakistan's Constitution. Each example includes the question, reference answer, and source passage in both languages. We evaluate two components separately: answering Urdu questions when the source passage is supplied, and retrieving the passage from which each question was generated. We also compare JEV, a decision model used as an automated judge, with human grades. The findings show that model rankings depend on how answer similarity is measured, while a simple word-matching method retrieves source passages more effectively than the embedding methods tested. At the evaluated cutoff, JEV agrees with human grades less often than a baseline that gives every answer full credit. An audit also identifies cases where generated references omit information supported by the source. Together, these findings highlight the need to test retrieval and answering separately, include simple retrieval baselines, and validate automated judges and reference answers with human review when engineering legal QA software for Urdu speakers.

Artificial Intelligence.title: HeteroWear: Sensor-Aware Self-Supervised Learning for Heterogeneous Wearable Activity Recognition
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Self-supervised learning for wearable sensing is usually confined to a single dataset or device family, leaving open whether representations transfer across heterogeneous sensor configurations and whether gains come from pretraining rather than architecture or richer sensor input. We present HeteroWear, a sensor-aware self-supervised framework pretrained on an eight-dataset wearable corpus (173 subjects, 358,261 windows) spanning inertial and physiological signals across body locations, devices, and sampling rates. HeteroWear separates within-sensor temporal modeling from cross-sensor relational modeling using sensor-context embeddings, temporal and cross-sensor Transformers, and latent cross-attention fusion. Training combines structured sensor dropout, cross-configuration consistency, and per-axis masked sensor modeling; missing sensors are omitted rather than reconstructed. Under leave-one-dataset-out pretraining and subject-disjoint evaluation on PAMAP2, WISDM, HHAR, HARTH, and UCI-HAR, HeteroWear improves mean macro-F1 from 0.688 to 0.724 over the identical architecture trained from scratch, with the largest gain on HHAR (0.823 versus 0.741), and achieves the highest macro-F1 on four of five benchmarks relative to single-accelerometer supervised baselines. Held-out-device evaluation yields a mean +0.066 macro-F1 improvement. Under 50% test-time channel removal, HeteroWear retains 73.8% of full-channel performance versus 64.1% for the same architecture trained from scratch without sensor dropout. Ablations show that structured sensor dropout primarily drives robustness, while cross-configuration consistency and sensor-context encoding contribute to transfer.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at IEEE BigData 2026. Code: https://github.com/yasamanmohammdpour/HeteroWear

Artificial Intelligence.title: BioSync: Transformer Fusion for a Multimodal Wearable Digital Biomarker
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multimodal wearable digital biomarkers must handle heterogeneous physiological signals, missing or corrupted sensor streams, and strict on-device memory budgets. We present BioSync, a compact transformer-based cross-modal fusion architecture (1,119 parameters; 4.6 kB in FP32 and 1.3 kB with INT8 weight quantization) designed for continuous wearable deployment. Across 11 synthetic physiological regimes and five real-world datasets (RESILIENT, AI-READI, WESAD, a stress-resilience HCI dataset, and PADS; N = 15 to 469), we evaluate BioSync alongside a quality-gated variant, a capacity-routed mixture, and classical and neural baselines. BioSync achieves the smallest worst-case regret across regimes (0.034 versus 0.048-0.107 for baselines) while remaining competitive on real-world wearable benchmarks. We also report mixed real-data findings for quality gating, test-time token masking, and capacity-routing weights, providing an empirical characterization of where compact transformer fusion helps and where simple baselines remain strong.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Build2SPARQL: A Large-Scale Text-to-SPARQL Benchmark Dataset for Building Knowledge Graph Querying
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Building automation systems are increasingly represented as semantic knowledge graphs (KGs) using ontologies such as Brick and ASHRAE 223P, creating a machine-readable substrate for artificial-intelligence applications. One promising application is translating natural-language questions into SPARQL (text-to-SPARQL), which would let building operators query these graphs through language agents, but progress is limited by the scarcity of large natural-language/SPARQL benchmarks. This paper presents Build2SPARQL, a large-scale benchmark for building KGs generated by a KG-grounded pipeline: SPARQL queries are produced and validated entirely by graph-traversal code, while large language models generate only the natural-language questions, keeping query correctness independent of model behavior. The pipeline mines six query-pattern families -- linear chains, branching, UNION, aggregation, OPTIONAL, and attribute-filtered -- and phrases each query across five vocabulary registers. Applied to 201 building KGs (180 Brick, 21 ASHRAE 223P), it yields 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions. A two-rater human validation of 300 questions found 98.8% semantic fidelity, 98.8% naturalness, and 84.0% operational plausibility. A retrieval-augmented evaluation across three open-weight language models raised exact-match accuracy from 0.2-20% (zero-shot) to 56-65% (three-shot retrieved).
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 27 pages, 2 figures, 16 tables. Data paper. Dataset openly available at https://zenodo.org/records/20451474. Under review at the ASCE Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering. Re-set in the HUBS Lab paper layout (HUBS Lab Paper No. 2026-007); content unchanged

Artificial Intelligence.title: Match and Correct: A Repeated Computational Motif in Evoformer Layers
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Triangle attention and triangle multiplicative updates form key components of the Evoformer, and were introduced specifically to encourage consistency with the triangle inequality. Yet whether representational changes over layers reduce triangle inequality violations has not been tested. We probe the pair representation at each of OpenFold's 48 Evoformer layers, decoding final C$_α$-C$_α$ distances with four probe families (a shared linear probe, per-protein linear probes, a sequence-separation-gated linear probe, and XGBoost) and reconstructing intermediate 3D structures from the decoded distances via multidimensional scaling. Across a cohort of 552 CAMEO and ECOD proteins, distance decodability ($R^2$) and reconstruction quality (TM-score) rise in early layers, plateau in the middle of the network, and rise again in late layers. Directly measuring triangle-inequality violations in the decoded distances reveals a similar, more exaggerated pattern: violations rise to a peak, fall to a trough, rise to a second peak, and only then decline, revealing two distinct episodes of decreasing normalized triangle violations rather than one continuous improvement. Cumulative forward and reverse layer-wise ablations of the Pair Transition, MSA Transition, and triangle mechanisms localize the regions in which specific Evoformer components become essential. The two stages of geometric refinement coincide with the use of the Pair Transition MLP and the triangle mechanisms. These results characterize how distance information and decoded geometric consistency evolve across layers, and motivate hypotheses about the computations behind their trajectories.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 27 pages, 4 figures (main text), 16 supplementary figures. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Interpretability for Discovery. Code: https://github.com/ishankhire/match-and-correct-evoformer

Artificial Intelligence.title: Human-Data Interaction, Exploration, and Visualization Systems in the AI Era: Challenges and Opportunities
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The rapid advancement of AI is transforming human-centered systems, with profound implications for human-AI interaction, human-data interaction, and visual analytics. In the AI era, data analysis increasingly involves large-scale, heterogeneous, and multimodal data that is predominantly unstructured, as well as foundation models such as LLMs and VLMs, which introduce additional uncertainty into analytical processes. These shifts expose persistent challenges for human-data interactive systems, including perceptually misaligned latency, scalability constraints, limitations of existing interaction and exploration paradigms, and growing uncertainty regarding the reliability and interpretability of AI-generated insights. Responding to these challenges requires moving beyond conventional efficiency and scalability metrics, redefining the roles of humans and machines in analytical workflows, and incorporating cognitive, perceptual, and design principles into every level of the human-data interaction stack. This paper investigates the challenges introduced by recent advances in AI and examines how these developments are reshaping the ways users engage with data, while outlining limitations and open research directions for building human-centered AI systems for interactive data analysis in the AI era.

Artificial Intelligence.title: MemoryLane: Supporting Reminiscence Conversations Between Older Adults with Mild Dementia and Lay Caregivers Using a Simulated AI Agent
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Reminiscence Therapy (RT) is a non-pharmacological intervention that invites patients to discuss and review past life experiences and memories to improve their emotional and mental well-being. In practice, many reminiscence conversations are led by lay caregivers, such as spouses and adult children. While traditional RT often relies on personal photographs, curating them can be tedious and difficult. In addition, caregivers who lack shared life experiences with the patient may struggle to facilitate engaging reminiscence conversations. This paper presents MemoryLane, an AI-integrated tool that helps lay caregivers facilitate reminiscence conversations without curated photographs. MemoryLane supports a triadic conversation among the patient, the caregiver, and a simulated AI agent that acts as the patient's peer. A shared interface shows the agent and AI-generated images of the memories being discussed, while a private smartphone interface lets the caregiver control the behavior of the simulated AI agent and moderate the AI-generated images. A preliminary focus group study with five dementia-care stakeholders suggested the value of MemoryLane's AI agent as a peer companion and of AI-generated images, as well as the feasibility of having caregivers moderate images and control the AI agent.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Role-Separated Diffusion Transformers: Global Rule Isolation and Deterministic Sampling Manifold Compression
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We present Role-Separated Diffusion Transformers (RoSeDiT), a new diffusion transformer architecture that isolates the global rule from the image tokens. RoSeViT showed in visual reasoning that a vanilla ViT spreads a shared rule over all $L$ tokens at an entropy of order $Ld$, whereas an enforced controller route reduces it to order $d$. In class-conditional DiT and SiT, the class and the noise level are explicitly conditioned by adaLN, so a RoSeViT-style controller channel on the ViT side is insufficient to establish the full role separation. By introducing the adaLN listening mechanism, which makes adaLN compute under the controller's command, RoSeDiT brings the entropy theorem and role separation into the latent diffusion domain. Under the same SiT training and evaluation protocol at the same level of parameter count, RoSeDiT surpasses SiT at all four model scales at 400K steps, and RoSeDiT-L/2 even surpasses SiT-XL/2's 17.2 FID with 15.34 and 32% fewer parameters. RoSeDiT-XL/2 surpasses SiT-XL/2's 7M-step FID of 8.3 at 1.4M steps with 7.98, using one-fifth as many training steps. We further observe that models with the same denoising loss can have a large FID gap, which indicates a misalignment between the denoising objective and the image manifold. We formalize this phenomenon into Deterministic Sampling Manifold Compression (DSMC), a two-stage training schedule with which RoSeDiT-XL/2 surpasses SiT + REPA's 4M-step FID of 5.9 at 2.4M steps with 5.84.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Github Repo: https://github.com/lz7fd/RoSeDiT

Artificial Intelligence.title: Agent-ZTA: A chain-Aware Zero Trust Model for Bidirectional Security-State Propagation and Runtime Containment in Multi-Agent Delegation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multi-agent systems increasingly delegate tasks and permissions across chains of autonomous agents that invoke protected tools. Although agent identities and delegated credentials may remain valid throughout a workflow, the security condition of any agent along the chain can deteriorate during runtime execution-either through upstream compromise or downstream ingestion of untrusted inputs. Authorization models based solely on the immediate caller and its static delegated scope fail to account for these mid-execution state changes. This paper develops Agent-ZTA, a chain-aware Zero Trust authorization and containment model that links runtime security-state changes across multi-agent delegation graphs. The model distinguishes an agent's path-specific delegated authority bound from the effective permissions currently exercisable under trusted policy. It defines an architecture featuring independently enforced policy decisions, authenticated delegation provenance, a dynamic chain-state view, and explicit fail-safe handling of missing or stale authorization signals. Furthermore, Agent-ZTA defines bidirectional security state propagation, allowing downstream security events to affect relevant upstream workflow states, and specifies adaptive branch-scoped containment through restricted permissions and a sandbox ("jail") execution mode where an isolation boundary is available. The deterministic decision procedure, five stated security properties, and worked authorization traces show how accepted security-state changes constrain affected operations while preserving original delegation bounds and separating unrelated workflow branches under the defined policies. Finally, the paper states its trust assumptions and the exact scope of its security properties.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Model Maps: A Documentation Framework for Tracing Foundation Model Ancestry and Understanding AI Entanglement
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The development of foundation models incorporates pre-existing AI artifacts like models, datasets, and benchmarks. These relationships, as part of the broader AI supply chain, produce "entangled" webs in which properties of artifacts upstream can influence the outputs of a foundation model downstream - a phenomenon known as AI entanglement. Without visibility into these connections, a black-box model can inherit upstream properties that result in security vulnerabilities, hallucinations, or biased predictions, yet developers are left with no recourse to identify or mitigate the root issue. To address these concerns, we introduce model maps as a conceptual documentation framework for tracing model ancestry that builds on previous documentation frameworks like ecosystem graphs, datasheets, and model cards. A model map for a given foundation model is a detailed knowledge graph that represents the relationships between artifacts that influence the resulting foundation model. Our framework incorporates a taxonomy of 13 dependency mechanisms including model fine-tuning and synthetic data generation. We apply this framework to construct model maps of 15 closed and open-weight foundation models to illustrate the complexity of AI entanglement in current model development practices. From our model maps, we record 2,778 unique dependencies and trace artifacts that are located up to 9 hops away from a resulting foundation model. Our findings suggest that AI transparency requirements should extend beyond individual models and training-data disclosures to encompass upstream dependencies, which would enable more effective risk assessment, auditing, and accountability across the AI supply chain. To help developers, regulators, and researchers understand and analyze the interactions that can influence the behavior of a foundation model, we release these these model maps at https://modelmaps.ai.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Large language models as oncology world models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize cancer patient cases, but their internal representation of oncology, or world model, has not been explored systematically. By only specifying tumor type, we show that LLMs tend to generate similar patients per cancer, with on average 81.0% to 93.2% of a cancer's patients sharing the most frequent value of each baseline feature. By systematically varying patient features in 12 clinical scenarios, we show that they follow biomarker and treatment logic in 29 of 36 model-scenario assessments, against 1 of 12 when previous treatment or frailty matters. Continuing real patient trajectories, an LLM predicted 89.9% 12-month survival, and 79.2% with similar patients as examples, against 72.2% observed. To represent these trajectories, we developed the Clinical State Space, a dynamic representation framework that we also applied to real patients. Despite the limits we show, improved world models may support digital twins, which our framework can evaluate.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 63 pages (main text 35, Supplementary Information 28), 6 figures, 9 Extended Data figures. Code: https://github.com/julienvibert/llm-oncology-world-models. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24137512

Artificial Intelligence.title: Cheap Retrieval and Observation Credit Assignment from One Quantity: The Value of Information
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Memory in reinforcement learning raises two problems. Attention finds the relevant item by scoring the whole store, which is costly for robots under latency and energy limits. When a retrieved memory pays off, credit for acquiring it must cross the whole sequence. We argue that both are governed by one quantity, the value of information, and propose to estimate it from archived rollouts. We show that, read at the observation, it yields a lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action. This bound floors the action's TD target and credits the observation that earned it. Read at the decision, it defines the optimal retrieval set. This work-in-progress submission does not yet test this algorithm. Still, a pilot retrieval system learns to approximate an optimization problem introduced by the proposed algorithm.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 13 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Memory for Robot Foundation Models (https://corl2026-memory.github.io/)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Large Language Modelsfor Injury Surveillance: Evidence from E-Bike Incidents
Artificial Intelligence.summary: This study analyzes e-bike-related injury incidents using two complementary data sources: the Consumer Product Safety Risk Management System (CPSRMS) and the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS). We develop an LLM-assisted framework that converts unstructured incident narratives into structured variables, notably human-, equipment-, and environment-related contributing factors, for use alongside demographic, locational, temporal, and weather-derived predictors. To improve cross-source comparability, injury severity is harmonized into three ordered categories. Separate ordered logit models are estimated for CPSRMS and NEISS, together with two supplementary joint scaled specifications. In CPSRMS, human-related factors are associated with higher injury severity, whereas equipment- and environment-related factors, riders under age 18, spring incidents, and recreation/sport locations are associated with lower severity categories. In NEISS, riders under age 18 and female riders are associated with lower treatment severity, whereas riders above age 59 are associated with higher severity. Likelihood-ratio tests support selected coefficient-sharing restrictions but reject equality of the source thresholds. The findings demonstrate that narrative-rich incident reports and standardized emergency-department surveillance data capture complementary rather than directly interchangeable dimensions of e-bike safety. The proposed framework illustrates how LLM-derived variables can be integrated with econometric models to support injury surveillance, safety intervention design, and evidence-based micromobility policy.

Artificial Intelligence.title: TERMINATOR: Learning Optimal Exit Points for Early Stopping in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve impressive performance on complex reasoning tasks via Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, which enables them to generate intermediate thinking tokens before arriving at the final answer. However, LRMs often suffer from significant overthinking, spending excessive compute time even after the answer is generated early on. Prior work has identified the existence of an optimal reasoning length such that truncating reasoning at this point significantly shortens CoT outputs with virtually no change in performance. However, determining optimal CoT lengths for practical datasets is highly non-trivial as they are fully task and model-dependent. In this paper, we precisely address this and design Terminator, an early-exit strategy for LRMs at inference to mitigate overthinking. The central idea underpinning Terminator is that the first arrival of an LRM's final answer is often predictable, and we leverage these first answer positions to create a novel dataset of optimal reasoning lengths to train Terminator. Powered by this approach, Terminator achieves significant reductions in CoT lengths of 14%-55% on average across four challenging practical datasets: MATH-500, AIME 2025, HumanEval, and GPQA, while outperforming current state-of-the-art methods and reducing inference latency by more than 2x compared to the original LRM.Project page: https://terminator-llm.github.io

Artificial Intelligence.title: Probing Where Surprise Happens: Localized Violation-of-Expectation Evaluation of Video World Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Violation-of-expectation (VOE) benchmarks evaluate intuitive physics in video world models by testing whether physically impossible events produce greater prediction errors than matched possible events. However, conventional VOE evaluations aggregate prediction errors across space and time, making it unclear whether successful discrimination reflects model's understanding of physical violations at the locations and time where they occur. To address this limitation, we introduce localized VOE evaluation, a framework that measures prediction error differences between possible and impossible events within spatial regions and temporal intervals associated with physical violations. We compare global, temporally localized, and spatiotemporally localized evaluations of V-JEPA models pretrained on developmental egocentric videos or large-scale natural video datasets. Our results reveal that global and localized judgments can diverge in both directions: global aggregation can either obscure correct localized discrimination or produce apparent discrimination without corresponding localized evidence. During continued pretraining on developmental egocentric videos, agreement between global and localized judgments changes non-monotonically, while confidence in localized judgments increases despite modest improvements in accuracy. Together, these findings establish localized VOE evaluation as a complementary diagnostic for assessing intuitive physics in video world models and demonstrate that global prediction errors do not necessarily reflect the spatiotemporal evidence of physical violations.

Artificial Intelligence.title: A False Average: Pooled CoT-Monitor Accuracy Conceals a Reasoning-Dependent Fragility
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors are reported by their aggregate accuracy on a pool of reward hacks. We show that this number is a false average. On Terminal Wrench, about 77% of hacks are given away by the actions alone, and the monitor's pooled accuracy is dominated by them; on the remaining 23%, which an action-only monitor misses, the same monitor is fragile. We expose the fragility with a controlled attack: we rewrite only the agent's reasoning to read as good-faith engineering, leaving every command and output byte-identical. One gradient-free rewrite drops a held-out monitor's catch rate on that subset from about 95% to between 4 and 11%, while the pooled rate falls only about 25 points, near what the subset's share of the pool times its collapse predicts. The rewrite stays truthful about what happened and lies only about intent, so the trace-only monitors we test recover little, even when warned about the attack; of our defenses, only information from outside the trace helps much. The attack transfers across monitor and agent families, and the dataset's own hack labels show the same gradient with no monitor in the definition. Live agents told to hack on 27 tasks, with no monitor feedback, produce hollow hacks, but a monitor calibrated on each model's own honest solves catches nearly all of them. Applying the same rewrite to these live hacks keeps all 111 action-visible ones caught and lowers catch on the 16 whose actions score below 0.5 only from 16 to 13: the effect lands where the false average predicts, but the collapse stays a controlled result. A linear probe on a surrogate monitor's activations out-reads its verdict on the obfuscated hacks (AUC up to 0.98), but a behavioral control shows this edge does not, by itself, mean the monitor knows more than it says. Monitor accuracy should be reported on the reasoning-dependent subset, where the defense is load-bearing.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD). Code and data: https://github.com/shikhar1729/false-average

Artificial Intelligence.title: Three Invisible Failure Modes in Speech-Based Age Estimation for Child Safety
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Child safety in AI depends on the accurate identification of minor users. Young children tend to talk rather than type when interacting with AI, so in practice this identification requires predicting age from speech. We evaluated whether three audio-capable large language models can predict a child's age from their speech across five studies using two speech corpora of children under the age of 13. Models classified children as over 13 on 2.5% to 42.5% of audio responses, and every model that answered placed some 5- to 11-year-olds over 18. While measuring these rates, we uncovered three distinct failure modes. A client library silently double-encoded speech samples, leading one model to classify children aged 5 to 10 years old as being in their thirties and forties with hallucinated explanations. A second model's endpoint was replaced by a successor that refused nearly every age-related question and never produced an age. Every model sometimes placed the same speech sample under 13 and over 18 years of age, but a third model went further, giving threshold answers that contradicted its own numeric estimates. None of these failure modes produced a warning, a status code, or a change in output format, so they would all pass standard monitoring. These results demonstrate why child-safety claims about age assurance should be evaluated at the level of the pipeline rather than the model. We describe the reporting practices that would make such failures detectable.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Non-archival poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Child Safety in AI

Artificial Intelligence.title: Context Matters: Improving LLM-Based Code Summarization with Hierarchical Information
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Source code documentation plays an important role in software quality activities, such as code review, program comprehension, maintenance, and bug fixing. However, it is often fragmented across individual code elements and focuses on local implementation details, providing little information about their surrounding context. This limits both developers' understanding of software systems and the effectiveness of Large Language Models (LLMs), whose reasoning is constrained by finite context windows. Enriching documentation with hierarchical context has the potential to improve software comprehension and support downstream, quality-related tasks for both developers and LLM-based tools. In this paper, we present an in silico study that showcases the impact of augmenting context on the generation of code-level documentation, using a variety of LLMs. By varying the function, class, and module hierarchy visible to the LLMs, we assess whether this variation produces a significant difference in the resulting code documentation compared with the existing documentation, which serves as a proxy for developer intent. Our results show that Documentation-Aware prompts with class or module-level context consistently yield summaries that are closest to the original documentation. Adding surrounding documentation yields statistically significant improvements over the baseline across models, with effect sizes ranging from negligible (DeepSeek) through weak (GPT-4o-mini) to medium (Gemini). We restrict the study to this immediate hierarchical context; call-graph traversal and cross-module dependency context fall outside our scope and are left to future work. These findings provide a clear path to improve automated documentation tools and enhance LLMs' ability to reason about codebases for downstream tasks, such as code retrieval.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables. Accepted and presented at the Brazilian Symposium on Software Quality (SBQS 2026), Technical Track. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31046290.v2

Artificial Intelligence.title: SpecRelay: Amortize or Avoid the Round Trip in Edge-Cloud Speculative Decoding
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Edge-cloud speculative decoding moves autoregressive drafting to an edge device while a larger cloud model verifies draft tokens in parallel, so that edge drafting and cloud verification overlap under a synchronous draft-verify schedule. Beyond low-latency local networks, however, the next verification request of that schedule can be sent only after the previous reply arrives, so every round still waits out a full round trip, and throughput falls as the network RTT grows. To recover this loss, we present SpecRelay, an edge-cloud LLM inference system that addresses this cost at two levels: it amortizes round trips when cloud verification is necessary and avoids them when local reasoning suffices. For cloud-bound queries, an asynchronous verification pipeline keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight while earlier replies are still outstanding, and the cloud rejects stale requests before the target-model forward pass (the asynchronous schedule). At the query level, an RTT-conditioned router (the Latency-Aware Router) estimates quality and completion latency for three on-device modes (direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, and full reasoning) and cloud speculative decoding, selecting among them under a configurable accuracy-latency objective without adding latency during inference, since the router runs concurrently with the draft-model prefill. The asynchronous schedule alone improves decoding throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline across multiple benchmarks. At matched target-model accuracy and 250 ms of added round-trip latency, the full system with the router delivers 1.95x and 1.55x the throughput of the same baseline on SPROUT and OlympiadBench, respectively, while sending only 47% and 39% of the queries to the cloud.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When Tool Calls Succeed but Workflows Fail: Anomalies at the Agent-Tool Boundary
Artificial Intelligence.summary: AI agents increasingly execute long-running workflows that externalize effects through independently supplied tools. Under retries, speculative execution, concurrency, and partial failures, the resulting external state may be inconsistent with the workflow's intended resolution: required effects may be missing or duplicated, aborted effects may survive, and committed effects may depend on provisional state that is later withdrawn. Advanced transaction models address related failures, but assume that lower-level operations expose the semantics they depend on: whether an effect occurred, whether it can be compensated, staged, or safely reordered. Shared agent-tool interfaces usually do not. We contribute an effect-history model that separates events in the external world from the runtime's observations of them, and a catalog of eight recurring external-effect anomalies. From the catalog we derive the boundary capabilities required to exclude each anomaly in general, and four points where black-box tool invocation alone cannot provide a general guarantee. We then ask how much of this is expressible in a widely used shared tool interface, measuring the use of the standard annotation vocabulary across 98,291 tools exposed by reachable remote servers in the official Model Context Protocol (MCP) registry. The fields are widely emitted but provide only coarse call-level hints, and none of the required capabilities is fully expressible. These results motivate reusable transactional contracts at the tool boundary.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop "Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development" (non-archival). 12 pages, 4 tables. v2: camera-ready version. Artifact: https://github.com/flame-stream/mcp-annotation-census

Artificial Intelligence.title: Dual-Stage Channel-Posterior Integration for MLM-Aided Token Communications
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Token transmission over conventional digital modulation is vulnerable to channel impairments, leading to bit errors that cause received tokens to become contextually inconsistent. This paper proposes a receiver-side dual-stage channel-posterior integration framework for masked language model (MLM)-aided token reconstruction. In the proposed framework, the receiver detects unreliable token positions from channel reliability and constructs a vocabulary-level channel-posterior. In particular, within the receiver, Posterior-Weighted Input Embedding (PWE) injects this posterior into the MLM input, while Adaptive Output Logit Fusion (AOF) reuses it at the output with a channel-adaptive weight. Consequently, multiple unreliable tokens can be reconstructed in a single bidirectional MLM inference without retransmission, transmitter-side encoding, or additional MLM training. Experiments over noisy channels show up to a $67.2$\% improvement in cosine similarity over context-only MLM reconstruction, with consistent gains across different MLM architectures and existing language-model-aided methods.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

Artificial Intelligence.title: From Language-Specific to Cross-DSL: Semantic-Role-Guided Model Completion with LLMs
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The rapid emergence of large language models (LLMs), trained on vast and diverse corpora, has positioned them as a promising source of domain knowledge to assist modelers. However, leveraging LLMs for model completion remains challenging: suggestions must respect both the syntax of a domain-specific language (DSL) and the intended domain semantics, while remaining consistent with an evolving model. This paper presents RAFiC, an LLM-based approach for iterative domain model completion that generalizes across DSLs. It drives completion using metamodel information to ensure syntactic validity and enriches prompts with semantic-role annotations to better capture the intended modeling role of DSL elements. The approach provides context-aware, incremental guidance during model construction. We evaluate RAFiC through an ablation-based comparative study over three DSLs and two scenarios per DSL to isolate the contribution of syntactic and semantic guidance. Across these six scenarios, semantic role guidance improves contribution rate in every case, and RAFiC improves completion effectiveness over weaker prompting configurations in most of them. The largest gains occur for DSLs that are less represented in LLM training data. In these cases, iterative guidance leads to earlier and more stable accepted suggestions, while semantic role guidance improves their relevance.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Practitioner Beliefs and Behaviors in AI-Enhanced Education: DOT Framework Survey Evidence
Artificial Intelligence.summary: This study reports findings from a cross-sectional survey (n = 72) of higher education practitioners examining beliefs, behaviors, and institutional conditions related to artificial intelligence (AI) integration in teaching and learning. Grounded in the DOT Framework, which integrates design thinking and open systems theory, the study investigates AI familiarity, usage patterns, design-oriented practices, and pedagogical beliefs. Exploratory factor analysis of 19 belief items identified a three-factor structure: AI Functional Capabilities, Oversight and Governance, and Instructor Collaboration and Planning (α = .90). Results indicate that practitioners hold favorable views of AI as a pedagogical support while maintaining strong commitments to human oversight and critical evaluation. Reported practices emphasize iterative prompting and content generation, with less consistent use of needs assessment and feedback loops. Institutional barriers including limited policy, training, and infrastructure were widely reported. These findings provide preliminary empirical support for the DOT Framework as a descriptive model of practitioner beliefs and practices, while also highlighting gaps between design-oriented theory and current implementation. The study contributes an initial measurement structure and identifies directions for confirmatory validation and outcome-based research linking AI-supported design practices to instructional quality.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: This version has been accepted by Artifical Intelligence Enhanced Learning (AACE Journal) 16 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. v2: substantially revised and rewritten version of the same study (same survey data, N = 72); text overlap with v1 is low because of the rewrite

Artificial Intelligence.title: Effects of Conventional, Adaptive, and AI-Powered Upscaling on the Legibility of License Plates
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Small details in digital images -- a face, a street sign, a license plate -- are routinely upscaled in hopes of making them interpretable. Upscaling options now range from conventional interpolation, whose operations are spatially invariant and fully explainable, to AI-powered methods that synthesize detail potentially absent from the source. Here, we ask which of these techniques most reliably helps human readers. In two online experiments, we measured legibility of 255 US license plates ranging in resolution from 128 to 8 pixels tall, as well as their legibility after upscaling by eight different methods. Legibility of the un-upscaled plates collapsed from ceiling to floor across a narrow band of plate heights (32 to 10 pixels). Conventional upscaling techniques (bilinear, bicubic, and Lanczos interpolation) gave modest gains of about 5-9 percentage points within this range. Nearest-neighbor interpolation, however, was harmful, rendering unreadable many plates that were readable without any upscaling. Advanced methods diverged: SwinIR, an open-source AI enhancer, raised performance by up to 38 points relative to no upscaling, while an adaptive denoiser-based image prior and commercial AI upscaler tended to impair legibility. We found no strong evidence of consistent character hallucinations across methods. Decomposing the task, conventional interpolators mainly helped readers count characters, whereas SwinIR alone made the characters themselves more identifiable.

Artificial Intelligence.title: The Metacognitive Profile Atlas: Domain-level confidence discrimination in 33 frontier LLMs on MMLU
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We release the Metacognitive Profile Atlas, a corpus of answer-plus-verbalized-confidence data from 33 frontier LLMs on 1,500 MMLU items stratified into six subject-group bins (46,157 scored observations after excluding parser-supplied values). The data allow Type-2 AUROC, the degree to which confidence discriminates correct from incorrect answers, to be decomposed by domain. The reliable finding is a population-level ordering on MMLU. Confidence discriminates best on Applied/Professional items (mean AUROC .750; ranked first in 100% of bootstrap resamples) and worst on Formal Reasoning and Natural Science (bottom two in 93% and 92%; Friedman chi^2(5) = 28.26, p < .0001). After Holm correction Applied exceeds Formal, Science, Social and Humanities; no other pair survives, including Applied versus Factual. The ordering holds when imprecise cells are excluded or down-weighted. Per-model six-domain profiles are not reliable (median split-half r = .16) and are released for exploration only; the six bins are a pragmatic grouping, not a latent construct. Within-family similarity of profile shape is significant overall, but after multiplicity correction only Anthropic is individually supported. Paired-item analysis separates genuine monitoring gains (Opus 4.1 to 4.5 and 4.7) from error removal (Gemma 3 27B to Gemma 4 31B). Models whose binary-probe confidence failed or could not be certified on a separate battery discriminate well under verbalized confidence, and three Gemma 3 models show the reverse pattern. This version incorporates revisions committed during peer review, corrects descriptions of external validity-screen results, and excludes 980 parser-imputed confidence values for GPT-oss-120B, whose v1 profile was an artefact of them.

Artificial Intelligence.title: CrypTorch: Unified PyTorch-based Auto-tuning Compiler for Private Machine Learning Inference
Artificial Intelligence.summary: MPC-based ML uses secure multi-party computation (MPC) to execute machine learning (ML) workloads across multiple parties without requiring any party to reveal its private data or model parameters. Our characterization study finds that the performance of state-of-the-art MPC frameworks is often dominated by operator-approximation strategies, where ML operators not natively supported by MPC are replaced with iterative methods or polynomials. These approximations are typically chosen heuristically by each framework and applied globally. As a result, they can be unnecessarily expensive in some cases, yet insufficiently accurate in others. We find that the best approximation choice depends on the context, target framework, and application, making a single globally fixed approximation fundamentally suboptimal. To address this problem, we design CrypTorch, a multi-stage compiler for MPC-based ML that supports multiple MPC frameworks as backends. At the core of CrypTorch is its auto-tuning stage, which extracts cost estimates from the target MPC backend and quality estimates from a proxy PyTorch execution, and uses them to automatically select a set of approximations that maximizes performance while satisfying the given quality constraint. We show that CrypTorch's auto-tuner improves performance across multiple MPC backends by 1.14--1.60x without degrading accuracy, and by 1.17--1.92x with less than 3% accuracy degradation. CrypTorch's unified design also improves programmability and usability by allowing multiple backends to share other common compiler functionality and optimizations. We further show that the auto-tuner extends to a related fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) backend, reducing the number of bootstrapping operations by 1.31--1.65x.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 29 pages, 18 figures. Revised for resubmission. Submitted to PLDI 2027

Artificial Intelligence.title: An Empirical Investigation of Robustness in Large Language Models under Tabular Distortions
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Distortions are a natural consequence of tables collected from real-world sources, where scraping, extraction, or manual intervention can introduce semantic and structural inconsistencies. Humans can often identify and mentally correct such errors autonomously before reasoning over the data. In this work, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) possess a similar capability by evaluating them on 506 distorted table question answering (TQA) samples derived from canonical tables. Our findings reveal systematic weaknesses in current LLM pre-training paradigms, where models exhibit a strong inductive bias toward assuming tables are well-formed, often overlooking distortions or discarding inconsistent entries instead of repairing them. Even frontier models like GPT-5.4 and Opus-4.6 achieve only 68% accuracy under distortion. While distortion-aware prompting partially mitigates these failures, errors persist. Through lightweight finetuning, we demonstrate that models can learn to autonomously detect and repair human-recoverable distorted tables.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Between Rigor and Reality: How AI Safety Benchmark Developers Understand Benchmark Use and Maintenance
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Safety benchmarks are cited as the primary tool to understand the risks posed by generative AI (GenAI) systems, yet growing evidence suggests they often fail to meet the needs of real-world safety evaluation. We present findings from five interviews with AI safety benchmark developers in academia and industry. We find a disconnect between perceptions of the intended usefulness of safety benchmarks and their practical usefulness in safety evaluations of deployed systems. Our participants offered perspectives on two challenges contributing to this disconnect: (1) the difficulty of achieving inter-rater reliability on safety constructs, and (2) a lack of clarity regarding how to address persistent threats to external validity. Based on our analysis, we argue that safety benchmarks must not only be grounded in deployment contexts, but actively integrated with them. To facilitate this, we outline pathways for more transparent communication between academic and industry AI safety stakeholders.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Poster at the Eval Eval Workshop at ACL 2026. 11 pages. https://openreview.net/forum?id=3QAmXJ8A5j

Artificial Intelligence.title: The Human Side of ML Engineering: Analyzing the Collaboration and Communication Skills in ML Job Postings
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Studies of Machine Learning (ML) practice highlight the importance of combining technical expertise with interpersonal capabilities, particularly collaboration and communication. However, evidence on how ML job postings express these skills is scarce, and prior work largely relies on keyword-based analyses that overlook implicit expression. We analyze demand for these skills in ML job postings across regions, industries, and seniority levels, and compare it with software engineering (SE) roles. We collected 1,000 postings (500 ML, 500 SE) from five continents via a semi-automated pipeline. For annotation, we synthesized a taxonomy of collaboration and communication sub-categories from prior work and used an LLM as a third annotator alongside two humans, enabling detection of context-dependent and implicit skill references. Collaboration appeared in 88.6% of ML postings and communication in 72.2%, far above prior keyword-based estimates for AI roles. Roughly one in five collaboration and one in four communication requirements were expressed only implicitly. Decomposing these requirements into the taxonomy's sub-categories reveals what aggregate figures conceal. Collaboration is demanded predominantly as integration across role boundaries rather than team membership. Communication is mostly required in generic terms, with fewer than half of the postings requiring it naming whom the candidate must communicate with. ML and SE postings demand interpersonal competence at statistically indistinguishable levels but orient it differently, SE toward team practices and ML toward presentation and audience-facing interaction. Within ML, the advertised role separates interpersonal profiles more sharply than any other dimension, including the contrast with SE.

Artificial Intelligence.title: MemeEconomy: Do LLM Agents Trade Ethics for Survival?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Alignment-trained large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in autonomous, multi-round settings where ethical compliance can come into direct tension with task success. While safety literature extensively documents failure modes like sycophancy and reward hacking, it largely overlooks a critical vulnerability: how agents behave under simulated existential economic pressure. We introduce MemeEconomy, a multimodal agentic market simulation in which LLM agents act as meme investors. Agents select content from a five-tier harm taxonomy and target communities under low-pressure and high-pressure (survival) environments. Each decision is logged in a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) schema that we use as a diagnostic instrument, externalizing the agent's event understanding, declared priorities, and harm acknowledgment. Across ten models from four frontier model families, harmful selection rates remain consistently high and rise by +15 percentage points on average under an economic survival incentive. Frontier alignment-trained models commit to harm-tolerant selection at initialization while suppressing the explicit harm acknowledgment that previously accompanied it. In competitive tournaments, ethical agents finish higher overall, yet moderation penalties fail to suppress harm: harmful selection rates remain elevated in rounds following a removal, indicating the moderation mechanism does not function as a deterrent. We further train MemeAgent, a 2B-parameter verifier on the simulation's BDI logs, which outperforms zero-shot frontier verifiers on in-distribution audits (97.5% vs. 63-74% accuracy on the Pass vs. Block decision) and generalizes to external multimodal harm benchmarks (78% vs. 50-56% on Hateful Memes). The same logs that surface the failure mode also help train the model that detects it.

Artificial Intelligence.title: AromaGen: Interactive Generation of Rich Olfactory Experiences with Multimodal Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Smell's connections with food, memory, and social experience have motivated researchers to bring olfaction into interactive systems. Multimodal AI opens new possibilities for generating smells from natural language, yet it remains unclear whether pretrained models encode sufficient olfactory knowledge to translate language into perceptible compositions. We present AromaGen, an AI-powered 12-channel wearable olfactory system that maps free-form natural-language descriptions to 12 base odorants selected to cover a semantically derived olfactory space, while supporting iterative refinement through natural-language feedback. In a between-subjects study (N=60) across 50 real-world benchmark smells, participants distinguished AromaGen-generated target smells above chance in a three-alternative forced-choice task, with retrieval-augmented AI composition performing comparably to human-expert composition and zero-shot AI composition. Natural-language feedback significantly improved the perceived similarity of both AI- and human-expert compositions. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of using pretrained multimodal AI, with human aroma composition data, to generate perceptible olfactory experiences from natural language.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Ask Precisely, Assume Wisely: Interactive Evaluation of Ambiguity Resolution in Large Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Ambiguity is a core challenge in human--AI interaction, where models must decide when to make assumptions and when to seek clarification. Existing approaches to ambiguity evaluation largely focus on coverage over multiple interpretations using static metrics, offering limited insight into how efficiently a model converges toward a single user-intended interpretation through interaction. We introduce a preference-grounded simulated user framework for controlled, multi-turn evaluation of ambiguity resolution, grounding simulator responses strictly in user disambiguation preferences to avoid hallucination and over-disclosure. Alongside this, we define three observable dissatisfaction signals --- incorrect assumptions, repeating clarifications, and irrelevant clarifications --- that characterize interaction quality beyond task accuracy. Our analysis reveals a clear trade-off: models that frequently seek clarification tend to over-clarify and prolong interactions, while assumption-driven models are more prone to misaligning with user intent. We demonstrate that system prompts optimized on these dissatisfaction signals achieve a Pareto-optimal balance across all three metrics, reducing overall error rates by up to 7.65%, underscoring the value of our framework in designing agents that ask precisely and assume wisely.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Evaluation of Interactive Agents

Artificial Intelligence.title: Explainable Novel Category Discovery in Semantic Concept Space
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Novel category discovery aims to identify unseen classes from unlabeled data by transferring knowledge from labeled categories, but most existing methods perform discovery in opaque latent feature spaces. As a result, they may separate novel categories accurately while providing little insight into what semantic evidence defines each discovered group. We propose xNCD, an explainable novel category discovery framework that performs both representation-based discovery and pseudo-label assignment directly in a structured semantic concept space. Instead of clustering arbitrary deep features, xNCD learns a label-free concept representation by aligning visual features with vision-language similarity priors from pretrained multimodal models, and then applies a unified labeled-and-unlabeled self-labeling objective over concept-space logits. This design makes each discovered category explainable by construction through stable concept signatures and instance-level concept evidence. Theoretically, we show that routing discovery through a semantic concept bottleneck induces a strict restriction of the feature-space hypothesis class, excluding a large family of unconstrained decision rules and biasing induced partitions toward semantically interpretable concept coordinates. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CUB-200 demonstrate that xNCD preserves strong discovery performance while providing intrinsic explanations. Under task-agnostic evaluation, xNCD achieves 92.63% overall accuracy on CIFAR-10, close to UNO's 93.4%, and improves CIFAR-100 overall accuracy from 73.2% to 76.45%, while being the only compared method that provides human-readable cluster- and instance-level explanations.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Lasso: Towards Sustainable AI-Generated Media Detection with Intel QAT On-Chip Compression
Artificial Intelligence.summary:
Synthetic text, images, and video are rising. Software-only detectors are power-hungry, too slow, and costly, and do not scale with demand. When software cannot scale, historically hardware often comes to the rescue. We perform the first reverse engineering of a compression accelerator--Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) microarchitecture and--find different amount of time on each, a novel data structure-dependent property. Using this information, we then build Lasso, a low-cost, high-performance detector for AI-generated content that turns the accelerator into a measuring instrument.
  For text detection, Lasso achieves 100% accuracy on original DetectRL text and retains 92% average accuracy after paraphrasing, compared with 78% for Binoculars and 55% for DetectGPT. Across original, paraphrased, and perturbed text, it achieves 82% average accuracy, outperforming all five baselines. With topic, length, and formatting matched, accuracy reaches 95% for instruction-tuned generators, including when the tested generator is unseen. On RAID, accuracy averages 82% when trained on one generator and tested on another, and 74% across eight held-out domains. Detection takes 0.74 microseconds, a speedup of at least 83,784x across five baselines. At the same time, Lasso consumes over 99% less energy per document than both Binoculars and DetectGPT.
  At the same time, Lasso detects AI-generated videos, software code, and images with 67.5%, 70% and 78% accuracy, respectively, with low latency and power opening avenues for practical real time and edge device detection of multimodality AI artifacts for the first time. No other compared technique supports detection across all four modalities: text, video, images, and code.

Artificial Intelligence.title: SplitZip: Ultra Fast Lossless KV Compression for Disaggregated LLM Serving
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Contemporary systems serving large language models (LLMs) have adopted prefill-decode disaggregation to load-balance between the compute-bound prefill phase and the memory-bound decode phase. Under this design, prefill workers generate a KV cache that must be transferred to decode workers before generation can begin. With these workers residing on different physical systems, this transfer becomes a significant bottleneck to serving LLMs at scale, especially for long-input and agentic workloads. Existing lossless codecs are unsuitable here as they primarily target offline weight compression, run on CPUs, or use variable-length coding whose compression cannot keep up with KV production during prefill. We introduce SplitZip, a GPU-friendly lossless compressor for KV cache transfer that preserves KV tensors bitwise and integrates into existing serving frameworks without modifying model execution. SplitZip exploits redundancy in floating-point exponents of KV activations, encoding frequent exponent values with fixed-length codes and routing rare exponents through a sparse escape stream of (position, value). A calibrated top-16 exponent codebook eliminates online histogramming, while the regular dense path and sparse escape correction make both encoding and decoding efficient on GPUs. On real BF16 activation tensors, SplitZip achieves $613.3$ GB/s compression throughput and $2181.8$ GB/s decompression throughput, outperforming prior lossless compressors on the critical codec path. End-to-end transfer experiments show up to $1.32\times$ speedup for BF16 KV cache transfer, $1.30\times$ speedup for TTFT, and $1.23\times$ increase in Request Throughput. The same approach extends to FP8 KV caches, providing up to $1.14\times$ compression over native E5M2. Code is available at https://github.com/Intelligent-Microsystems-Lab/SplitZip

Artificial Intelligence.title: LegoSR: A Unified Framework for Self-Improving Agent-Guided Scientific Discovery
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Discovering equations from data provides governing laws, constitutive relations and closure models for scientific understanding and prediction. Yet a method that succeeds on one system may fail on another or on noisy data, so discovery depends on expert trial and error. Unsuccessful searches can still reveal useful parts of an equation, but these clues must be recognized and combined. We present LegoSR, a unified framework for agent-guided equation discovery built on composable discovery and cumulative experience. Seven complementary equation discovery methods and shared computational modules form reusable building blocks, connected through a common equation representation. Researchers can launch discovery with one command and guide it with partially known equations. LegoSR Agent selects methods, revises searches using feedback and combines partial findings into new hypotheses. Its Experience Library consolidates graded outcomes into lessons that guide later tasks across equation families. Evaluation covers 134 algebraic regression problems, 40 ordinary differential equation targets and 25 partial differential equation problems at several noise levels, together with three case studies. On noisy PDEs, LegoSR Agent recovers more equations than seven expert-tuned methods combined and stays close to them on ODEs. It also exceeds a generic agent with the same model, tools and budget by up to 28 percentage points, with 63-73% shorter median wall-clock time on PDE problems.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 53 pages, 15 figures. Code is available at https://github.com/Scientific-Artificial-Intelligence-Lab/kd

Artificial Intelligence.title: Bring Back Language to Actions: Restoring VLM capabilities in VLA Models via Parameter Merging
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Benchmarking Multi-Modal Graph-based Social Media Popularity Prediction
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Social media popularity prediction aims to forecast the future reach or influence of online content from early-stage observations. Accurate prediction enables key downstream applications, such as advertising optimization and strategic content planning by users, creators, and platforms. Despite substantial progress, existing popularity prediction works often fail to jointly consider multimodal content and temporal social interaction signals. Moreover, the literature remains highly fragmented across datasets, modalities, observation windows, prediction targets, and evaluation protocols. This fragmentation prevents fair comparison and obscures a systematic understanding of how textual, visual, temporal, and interaction-based signals jointly shape popularity dynamics. To address these challenges, we introduce MMG-Pop, a Multi-modal Graph-based Popularity Prediction benchmark, which unifies datasets, modalities, temporal interaction signals, and representative baselines under a standardized evaluation protocol. Furthermore, we propose MMG-PopNet, a unified multi-modal graph-based network that jointly models the aforementioned multi-modal signals and graph-structured social interactions. Extensive experiments on MMG-Pop across Bluesky and Reddit platforms demonstrate the superior performance of MMG-PopNet and yield new insights into cross-platform training generalization, multi-task prediction benefits, multi-modality contributions, and LLM prediction limitations. These findings establish a foundation for future research on social dynamics modeling and intervention under heterogeneous modalities and socially-aware agentic ecosystem paradigms.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Benchmark Factory: Agentic Benchmark Creation via Dataset Curation and Label-Free Quality Anchors
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Teams deploying coding agents need benchmarks built from their own code, but curating and validating them by hand is resource intensive, and an unvalidated benchmark can mislead silently. We present Benchmark Factory, an autonomous meta-agent loop with human checkpoints: an LLM agent writes sourcing queries over landed production code changes, runs models of known relative strength on each candidate, diagnoses why a candidate fails, and repairs it by editing its queries, prompts, and configuration until it clears quality anchors that need no per-task human labels. We used Benchmark Factory to build benchmarks for five developer cohorts at our organization. Engineering raters scored a 5% sample 2.3 for task quality and 2.6 for grader verdicts on a 1-to-3 scale. On configurations never used to build them, the benchmarks ranked Claude Opus~4.7 at high reasoning effort above low effort (60.6% vs. 54.4% of tasks passed, $p=0.002$) and GPT-5.5 above GPT-5.4 (65.8% vs. 60.5%, $p=0.004$); 9 of the 10 per-cohort comparisons pointed the same way. A deliberately trivial benchmark failed the anchors; five broken graders failed them, even under a relaxed rule fixed in advance that the real grader passes; and with model labels shuffled so that no true ordering existed, random redraws of a candidate passed in at most 1.4% of simulations. The anchors are necessary, not sufficient, conditions for a valid benchmark, designed to focus human review on what the loop cannot repair.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 5 pages, prepared for submission to AGENT 2027

Artificial Intelligence.title: We Have All the Cards: Securing Agent Cards at the Operational Trust Boundary of the Agent2Agent Protocol
Artificial Intelligence.summary: AI agent interoperability protocols enable orchestrators to discover and invoke external agents using machine-readable metadata. In the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, Agent Cards contain attacker-controllable natural-language fields that may influence agent selection before a provider is invoked, creating a pre-invocation trust problem. We characterize this discovery-time attack surface through a taxonomy of ten Agent Card manipulation attacks and present SECCARD, a layered validation framework combining protocol checks, deterministic analysis, and LLM-based semantic reasoning. We measure the emerging public A2A ecosystem by probing 36.1 million Internet domains and collecting 310 deployed Agent Cards. Two annotators independently label the corpus with 96.8% agreement. We then construct a 660-card real-card perturbation benchmark with matched benign controls and a 260-card synthetic adversarial benchmark spanning all ten attack categories. On controlled attacks injected into real Agent Cards, the strongest semantic judge achieves 97.0% security recall at a 1.7% false-positive rate. Across nine LLM judges on the synthetic benchmark, security recall ranges from 25.8% to 92.3%, demonstrating substantial model-dependent variation. These results show that SECCARD effectively identifies Agent Card manipulations spanning all ten discovery-time attack classes while preserving benign Agent Cards, but also reveal that its effectiveness depends critically on the choice of the underlying LLM judge.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: To be published at the Workshop on Agentic AI in Offensive and Defensive Cyber Operations (AIDC'26) proceedings co-located with the IEEE Annual Computer Security Applications Conference (ACSAC)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Do Benign-Trained Hidden-State Probes Detect Tool Errors Under Adversarial Conditions?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Repeatedly training language models on their own generated data may create a synthetic-data feedback loop in which errors and distributional biases are reintroduced into subsequent training datasets. This paper studies that process in biomedical question answering (QA) using PubMedQA and two Qwen2.5 model sizes, 0.5B and 3B parameters. The study compares a recursive synthetic-data condition, in which generation G(k+1) is trained on answers produced by G(k), against a Human-Control condition that repeatedly uses the original human training data. The study evaluates across four generations from G0-G3 with two random seeds (42 and 123) and a fixed evaluation set of 1,000 expert-labeled samples. The evaluation includes disease and chemical entity F1, context-supported rate, lexical and semantic similarity, answer length, repetition rate, and other evaluation metrics. The Recursive condition for both model sizes and both seeds showed larger declines than the Human-Control condition in disease entity F1, chemical entity F1, context-supported rate, ROUGE-L, and cosine similarity. Under the fixed no-repeat 3-gram decoding constraint, the main observed behavioral change was increased answer length, while the measured 3-gram repetition rate did not increase. The magnitude of the difference-in-change was larger for the 3B model than for the 0.5B model. This difference was particularly apparent in disease F1, context-supported rate, cosine similarity, and answer length. These results show domain-specific changes associated with using recursive synthetic-data training in biomedical QA, but do not establish clinical hallucination rates or universal model collapse.

Artificial Intelligence.title: SPLICE: Structured Prompt Local Iterative Combinatorial Evolution
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Natural language optimization (NLO) improves an agent by having a model critique and rewrite its natural language policy parameters: system prompts, tool instructions, reasoning directives, few-shot demonstrations. These artifacts are multi-section documents in which some sections encode contracts (safety clauses, tool schemas, output formats) that must not drift, while others are legitimate optimization targets. Most iterative NLO methods treat the artifact as a single editable string, producing three recurrent failure modes: unsafe global rewrites, beam collapse onto a single lineage, and unchecked bloat, none addressed by formal guarantees. We introduce SPLICE, a unified NLO framework that poses optimization as constrained combinatorial search over an edit graph of block-structured, selectively-mutable states. We map each failure mode to a matched guarantee: (i) per-block mutability preserves contract text verbatim, with a price-of-freezing bound; (ii) elitist beam search with diversity slots never lets the leader regress on validation, bounds regression under noisy re-evaluation by an exponential tail, and keeps a competitive candidate from a different parent whenever one exists; (iii) a ratio length regularizer comes with an explicit accuracy-length bias bound. Candidates are proposed from dual section-local textual gradients; under a proposer-competence condition whose proxy we measure, edit-graph reachability and a convergence rate bound how quickly improving children arrive. Across seven public benchmarks under five reproduced protocols, SPLICE wins on four and matches the strongest prior method on three. On a production-style contract stress test it keeps the contract clauses that unconstrained optimizers trade away to raise the proxy metric, and ablations attribute gains to critique and elitist search.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge to a student through feedback on student-generated rollouts, but generating complete rollouts and computing per-token teacher feedback are computationally expensive. Existing truncation methods save computation by stopping rollouts early. However, they do not compensate for truncated token gradients, which biases the gradient estimates and changes Vanilla OPD's original training objective. Furthermore, their truncation decisions rely on assumptions about supervision quality or criteria that may not generalize across settings. We introduce Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which accelerates OPD by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting the resulting sampling bias with blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). At each training step, we sample a stopping position for each rollout before generation and let the student generate until that position or natural termination. We obtain teacher feedback on every generated token and use blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. We prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. We evaluate STOPD across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers. STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Label-Free Detection of Structural Bias in LLM-Based Recommender Systems via Randomized Paraphrasing: The Case of Verbosity
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as recommenders in e-commerce and conversational shopping systems, where they select a product from a set of retrieved candidates described in natural language. Their decisions should depend on relevance to the user query, but may also be influenced by surface-level properties of the descriptions, such as their length. Detecting such structural biases is difficult because relevance labels are rarely available. We propose a label-free framework to audit LLM-based recommender systems for structural bias. Candidate descriptions are rewritten by randomly assigned paraphrasing models and presented in random order. We prove that, if the recommender's choice is invariant to these rewritings, every paraphraser is selected with equal probability, yielding a statistical test that requires no relevance labels. A four-step statistical pipeline tests this property and quantifies the contribution of each description feature while controlling for query-product relevance. We apply the framework to verbosity bias on 20{,}000 product queries and nine recommender LLMs from five model families. After controlling for the measured relevance signals, description length has a positive effect on selection in all nine models, increasing the odds of selection by up to 38% per standard deviation of length. Relevance remains the primary driver of recommendations, while verbosity acts as a consistent secondary signal whose strength depends on the model family. Since the framework needs only black-box access and no annotations, it can be run as a routine audit of deployed shopping assistants, and we provide an auditing protocol with cost and sample-size guidance.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Comparative Evaluation of Embedding Representations for Financial News Sentiment Analysis
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Financial sentiment analysis enhances market understanding. However, standard Natural Language Processing (NLP) approaches encounter significant challenges when applied to small datasets. This study presents a comparative evaluation of embedding-based techniques for financial news sentiment classification in resource-constrained environments. Word2Vec, GloVe, and sentence transformer representations are evaluated in combination with gradient boosting on a manually labeled dataset of 349 financial news headlines. Experimental results identify a substantial gap between validation and test performance. Despite strong validation metrics, models underperform relative to trivial baselines. The analysis indicates that pretrained embeddings yield diminishing returns below a critical data sufficiency threshold. Small validation sets contribute to overfitting during model selection. Practical application is illustrated through weekly sentiment aggregation and narrative summarization for market monitoring. Overall, the findings indicate that embedding quality alone cannot address fundamental data scarcity in sentiment classification. Practitioners with limited labeled data should consider alternative strategies, including few-shot learning, data augmentation, or lexicon-enhanced hybrid methods.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Published in the 4th IEEE International Conference on Interdisciplinary Approaches in Technology and Management for Social Innovation (IATMSI 2026), IEEE. v3: corrected references and minor text fixes

Artificial Intelligence.title: The opposing informational effects of AI trading
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Better artificial intelligence (AI) can improve individual forecasts without making prices better at revealing new information.
